title: Google Cloud Observability: Monitoring, Logging, Trace, Profiler
bodyMarkdown:
## The Google Cloud Observability toolbox

Google Cloud Observability gives you one product per question you ask about a running system. The exam repeatedly tests whether you can match the question to the tool.

| Question | Tool | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| Is it healthy? Is it within SLO? | Cloud Monitoring | Metrics, dashboards, alerting policies, uptime checks, SLOs |
| What happened? | Cloud Logging | Log entries, buckets, sinks, log-based metrics, audit logs |
| Where did the time go for this request? | Cloud Trace | Distributed tracing across services; spans retained 30 days |
| Which code burns CPU or memory? | Cloud Profiler | Continuous statistical profiling; profiles retained 30 days |
| Which exceptions are happening and how often? | Error Reporting | Groups errors by root cause |

## Cloud Monitoring

[Cloud Monitoring](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/docs/monitoring-overview) collects metrics from Google Cloud services automatically (system metrics), from VMs and third-party apps through the **Ops Agent**, from your own code (user-defined and custom metrics), and from Prometheus workloads through **Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus**. It provides Google-managed dashboards that appear for your resources, custom dashboards, alerting policies, uptime checks, and multi-project views through **metrics scopes** (a single scoping project can view metrics from many projects and AWS accounts).

Practical points:

- System metrics for managed services need no agent.
- On Compute Engine, in-guest metrics and logs come through the [**Ops Agent**](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/agents/ops-agent), the primary agent for VMs and the successor to the legacy agents. It uses Fluent Bit for logs and the OpenTelemetry Collector for metrics and traces (it accepts OTLP traces from instrumented apps). Out of the box it collects system metrics (CPU, disk, memory, network, processes) and syslog or `/var/log/messages` (Windows Event Log on Windows); third-party application metrics and logs are added by configuration. It is for **Compute Engine only**: the docs state it is not supported on Amazon EC2 instances or on-premises machines, and it is **not needed** on GKE, Cloud Run or App Engine, which have built-in collection. For everything else, see the next section.
- Use a metrics scope in a dedicated monitoring project to see a whole environment (for example many GKE clusters across projects) in one place. This is the standard answer for "centralize observability across projects".
- Notification channels include email, the Cloud Mobile App, PagerDuty and Slack, among others.

### Uptime checks

[Uptime checks](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/uptime-checks) are black-box probes of availability. Public checks send HTTP, HTTPS or TCP requests from multiple global locations to URLs, VMs, App Engine apps, Kubernetes services, AWS EC2 instances or Cloud Run revisions. Private checks reach resources on private networks. Details worth knowing: you need at least three checker locations selected, HTTP(S) checks follow redirects and evaluate the final response, and the default alerting setup notifies when at least two regions report failure for a minute or more. Public uptime checks are not supported inside VPC Service Controls perimeters. An uptime check tells you about outside-in availability; it does not tell you why something is slow.

### Alerting policies

[Alerting policies](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerts) support metric-threshold, metric-absence (missing data for up to 24 hours), forecasted metric-value (forecast windows of 1 to 7 days), PromQL and log-based conditions. Behavior worth remembering from the [alerting concepts](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerts/concepts-indepth) page:

- A **retest window** (duration) requires the condition to hold continuously before firing; longer means fewer false positives and slower detection.
- The default **auto-close** duration is seven days after data stops arriving, and incidents also close when the condition clears.
- A single policy can have at most 1,000 open alerts at a time.
- Alignment period should be no longer than 24 hours minus ingestion delay.
- Use **snoozes** to suppress notifications temporarily; policies stay active.
- Put documentation (runbook links, dashboards) in the policy so the notification is actionable.

### Dashboards as code and metrics scopes

Custom dashboards are JSON [`Dashboard` resources](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/dashboards/api-dashboard) you can manage with the console, gcloud, the API or Terraform, so they can be reviewed and versioned. To reuse one across projects, export it (`gcloud monitoring dashboards describe DASHBOARD_ID --format=json`), remove `name` and `etag`, and create it in each project from a pipeline with `gcloud monitoring dashboards create --config-from-file` or the Terraform `google_monitoring_dashboard` resource. A copy is a template, not data. Predefined (service-specific) dashboards cannot be retrieved through the API or copied, only their charts can be copied into a custom dashboard, and a Terraform-managed dashboard should not be edited in the console: change the JSON and re-apply. Dashboards live in the [scoping project](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/settings), so one view over many projects is a metrics scope: viewers need Monitoring Viewer on the scoping project only, while adding a project needs Monitoring Admin on both sides. A scope holds 375 projects by default.

## Collecting telemetry outside Google Cloud

For hybrid and multicloud estates the goal is **one plane**: every environment feeds Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging, so alerting policies, dashboards, SLOs and retention are defined once instead of running a second stack on-prem or in another cloud. Choose the collection path by where the workload runs:

| Where it runs | Collection path | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| GKE, Cloud Run, App Engine, Cloud Run functions | Built in | No agent; [stdout and stderr are collected](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/structured-logging) |
| Compute Engine VM | Ops Agent | Service account needs Logs Writer and Monitoring Metric Writer; [not supported on EC2 or on-premises machines](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/agents/ops-agent) |
| On-prem or other-cloud hosts and VMs | OpenTelemetry Collector, fleet-managed with [Bindplane](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/bindplane) | Bindplane is an OpenTelemetry-based pipeline Google documents for hybrid and on-premises collection |
| EKS, AKS or other conformant clusters registered to a fleet (attached clusters) | Fluent Bit-based logging agent run as a DaemonSet | [System logging is on by default; workload logging needs Kubernetes 1.23 or later](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/multi-cloud/docs/attached/aks/how-to/install-cloud-logging) |
| Prometheus-style metrics anywhere | [Managed Service for Prometheus](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/managed-prometheus) | Runs on GKE, non-GKE Kubernetes, other clouds and on-prem; 24 months in Monarch, PromQL queries, alerting through Cloud Monitoring |

Bindplane metrics land in the [same dashboards, charts and alerts](https://docs.cloud.google.com/monitoring/bindplane/collecting-on-prem-hybrid) as native ones.

**Authentication without exported keys.** Compute Engine uses an attached service account. Off Google Cloud, Google's [non-GKE collection guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/managed-prometheus/setup-managed) walks through a service account key with Monitoring Metric Writer stored as a Kubernetes secret, and an OpenTelemetry Collector writing logs, metrics and traces needs `roles/logging.logWriter`, `roles/monitoring.metricWriter` and `roles/telemetry.tracesWriter`. A long-lived key is the weakest option; [Workload Identity Federation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workload-identity-federation) lets on-premises or multicloud workloads (AWS, Azure, OIDC, SAML, X.509, Active Directory) use federated identities instead, and tools read its credential configuration file through [`GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workload-identity-federation-with-other-providers). When a scenario forbids exported keys, the answer is federation.

## Cloud Logging

Everything Cloud Logging does revolves around **log entries**, **buckets** and **sinks**. Ingested entries are routed by sinks. Two sinks exist in every project:

| Sink / bucket | Receives | Retention | Configurable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `_Required` | Admin Activity and System Event audit logs (and Access Transparency) | 400 days | Cannot be changed or deleted |
| `_Default` | Everything else, including Data Access and Policy Denied audit logs | 30 days | Retention and filter editable; sink can be disabled |
| User-defined bucket | Whatever your sinks send | 30 days by default | 1 to 3650 days |

Sources: [log buckets](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/buckets), [audit logs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit), and [routing overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/routing/overview). Notes: Admin Activity logs are always on and cannot be disabled; Data Access logs are off by default except for BigQuery. You can **lock** a bucket, which is irreversible: the retention policy becomes immutable and the bucket cannot be deleted until every entry has met its retention period. Bucket region is fixed at creation.

### Routing and aggregated sinks

A sink has an inclusion filter, optional exclusion filters, and a destination: a log bucket (including in another project), BigQuery dataset, Cloud Storage bucket, Pub/Sub topic, or another project. Exclusion filters apply after ingestion and do not reduce API quota use. Sinks are not retroactive: they route only entries created after the sink exists.

An [aggregated sink](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/aggregated_sinks) at the organization or folder level, with `includeChildren`, routes entries from all child projects to one place. Each sink has a **writer identity** that needs a destination role (Logs Bucket Writer, Storage Object Creator, BigQuery Data Editor or Pub/Sub Publisher). Up to 200 sinks per folder or organization. Intercepting aggregated sinks stop child-level routing (except to `_Required`).

The canonical compliance design is therefore: **organization-level aggregated sink, filtered to admin activity audit logs, into a dedicated, access-controlled destination (a locked log bucket with long retention, or Cloud Storage with a retention policy, or BigQuery for queries), outside the generating projects.** Raising `_Default` retention in every project is the wrong answer because it leaves logs in the projects that generate them and is not centrally governed.

### Structured logging and special fields

On GKE, Cloud Run, Cloud Run functions and App Engine flexible, an [integrated agent](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/logging) sends what the container writes to stdout or stderr. What you get depends on the format:

| Container writes | Result |
|---|---|
| One line of serialized JSON | `jsonPayload`; special keys are promoted to LogEntry fields |
| Plain text | `textPayload` with nothing to index; on GKE, [stdout is INFO and stderr is ERROR](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/about-logs) whatever the text says |
| JSON preceded by prefix text such as a timestamp | Not parsed as JSON |

The [special fields table](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/agent/logging/configuration#special-fields), which the Cloud Run docs point to, moves these keys out of `jsonPayload`: `severity`, `message` (the display line), `httpRequest`, `time`, and the prefixed `logging.googleapis.com/insertId`, `labels`, `operation`, `sourceLocation`, `spanId`, `trace` and `trace_sampled`. Consequences:

- **Severity filters and alerts need the key.** Without `severity`, a level filter, a log-based metric or an alert on ERROR cannot match, even though the entry arrived.
- **Trace correlation needs `logging.googleapis.com/trace`** set to `projects/PROJECT_ID/traces/TRACE_ID` (from the `X-Cloud-Trace-Context` header on Cloud Run). [Container logs are not correlated with request logs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/logging) unless you use a client library or this field.
- **Stack traces.** [Error Reporting](https://docs.cloud.google.com/error-reporting/docs/formatting-error-messages) accepts a multi-line `textPayload` or a `jsonPayload` whose `message`, `stack_trace` or `exception` field holds the trace. Keep the whole trace in one JSON field so it stays one entry.
- **On a VM the rules differ.** The Ops Agent only parses JSON if you configure a `parse_json` processor, its keys are the prefixed names (for example `logging.googleapis.com/severity`), and its [files receiver makes one entry per line](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/agents/ops-agent/configuration) unless you add a `parse_multiline` processor.
- **Missing entries are a different failure from wrong severity.** On GKE, duplicate JSON keys and a `stream` key can cause [dropped logs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/about-logs), an oversized `jsonPayload` entry is dropped (`textPayload` is truncated), and a node service account without `roles/logging.logWriter` produces [401 or 403 errors and missing logs](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/troubleshooting/logging).

### Log-based metrics

[Log-based metrics](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics) turn log entries into time series for charts and alerts. **Counter** metrics count matching entries; **distribution** metrics extract numeric values (for example latency) into histograms. System-defined ones are project level; **user-defined** ones are chargeable like custom metrics and can be scoped to a project or a log bucket (bucket scope helps with aggregated sinks). They only count entries received after the metric is created, so they are not retroactive, and the time series can contain zeros and gaps. The exam pattern: structured JSON logs contain a field for a business event, you need an alert on its rate, so create a counter log-based metric and alert on it. Exporting everything to BigQuery for a scheduled query, or extending retention, does not make the event alertable.

### Log Analytics

[Log Analytics](https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/log-analytics) lets you run **SQL** over log data (for example, group entries by hour and average latency) and join logs with trace data, which Logs Explorer cannot do. To use it, upgrade a project-level log bucket (it must be unlocked unless it is `_Required`, with no pending updates); entries written before the upgrade are backfilled, which can take several days. A **linked BigQuery dataset** gives read access to the same bucket data with no BigQuery ingestion or storage cost (queries are still billed), and you create one to join logs with other BigQuery data, use BigQuery Studio, use reserved slots or build SQL-based alerts. Caveats: it does not deduplicate entries as Logs Explorer does, and field-level access controls block it. Choose Log Analytics for ad hoc investigation and reporting without a second copy; use a sink to BigQuery when you need an independent, long-lived copy in another project. For a rate alert on an event, a counter log-based metric is still the standard path.

## Cloud Trace

[Cloud Trace](https://docs.cloud.google.com/trace/docs/overview) is distributed tracing: it measures end-to-end latency of a request and shows which downstream calls consumed the time. Google recommends instrumenting with **OpenTelemetry** (Go, Java, Node.js and Python samples) rather than proprietary client libraries. Some services, such as App Engine and Cloud Run, produce traces automatically; others need instrumentation. Traces correlate with logs, the Trace Explorer shows latency heatmaps, and spans are kept for 30 days. Use Trace when the symptom is "this request is slow and there are many services".

Google [recommends a vendor-neutral framework](https://docs.cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/instrumentation/overview) such as OpenTelemetry even if you only send telemetry to Google Cloud, so changing backends needs no code change. Export uses OTLP through the Telemetry API, a Google-built OpenTelemetry Collector runs on GKE, Cloud Run and Compute Engine, and Java workloads on GKE can use zero-code auto-instrumentation. The anti-pattern is hard-wiring a proprietary client library into every service.

## Cloud Profiler

[Cloud Profiler](https://docs.cloud.google.com/profiler/docs/about-profiler) is a statistical, low-overhead profiler that continuously gathers CPU and memory-allocation information from production. Profile types include CPU time, heap, allocated heap, contention, threads and wall time depending on language (Go, Java, Node.js, Python). Overhead is under 5% during collection and commonly below 0.5% amortized across replicas. Data is retained for 30 days. It runs on Compute Engine, GKE, App Engine and external systems, among others. Use Profiler when latency is fine but cost or CPU is high, or when you want to know which function to optimize. Trace answers "which service", Profiler answers "which function".

## Error Reporting

[Error Reporting](https://docs.cloud.google.com/error-reporting/docs/grouping-errors) aggregates and groups errors from the Error Reporting API or from stack traces found in Cloud Logging. Stack-trace errors are grouped by exception type and the five topmost frames. It samples up to 1,000 errors per hour (100 per hour under extreme load) and extrapolates counts. It analyzes log entries only when Assured Workloads is not enabled and the log buckets do not use CMEK, a detail that matters for regulated workloads.

## Newer tooling: Gemini Cloud Assist and App Hub

[Gemini Cloud Assist](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cloud-assist/overview) runs AI-driven investigations from logs, errors or natural-language prompts, can start an investigation automatically when an alerting policy fires, and lets you explore metrics, logs, alerts and errors in plain language. [App Hub](https://docs.cloud.google.com/app-hub/docs/overview) is the registry that groups services and workloads into **applications** with ownership and criticality metadata, so monitoring and troubleshooting are application-centric rather than per-resource. These accelerate diagnosis; they do not replace SLOs, alerting policies or instrumentation.

## Designing observability for a regulated, multi-cluster estate

For a scenario such as a healthcare provider with many GKE clusters plus on-prem systems, the usual combined answer is: a central monitoring project with a metrics scope and dashboards on golden signals and SLOs, structured logging with log-based metrics and organization-level sinks for audit and quality signals, and Trace plus Profiler to diagnose hotspots. The Four Golden Signals from the [SRE monitoring chapter](https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/) are **latency** (separating successful from failed requests), **traffic**, **errors** (explicit, implicit such as a 200 with wrong content, or by policy) and **saturation** (how full the most constrained resource is).

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Disabling logging to save money or "reduce attack surface".** Use exclusion filters, sampling and routing instead; audit logs are required for compliance and Admin Activity cannot be turned off.
- **Choosing Trace when you need Profiler, or the reverse.** Request path across services is Trace; code-level CPU and memory is Profiler.
- **Assuming log-based metrics back-fill.** They start at creation time.
- **Paging on causes.** The SRE guidance is that every page should be actionable and indicate users are affected; a high-CPU page that nobody acts on is noise.
- **Relying on uptime checks alone.** They are outside-in and binary; they do not replace SLO and golden-signal monitoring.
- **Extending `_Default` retention everywhere for compliance** instead of centralizing with an aggregated sink and a locked bucket.
- **Misplacing the Ops Agent.** Forgetting it on Compute Engine loses in-guest metrics and app logs; installing it on GKE, Cloud Run or App Engine is pointless (native collection); on-prem or EC2 hosts are unsupported, so use an OpenTelemetry Collector.
- **Running a second monitoring stack for hybrid sites** with its own alerting and retention, instead of sending everything to Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging.
- **Exporting a service account key for an off-cloud collector** when Workload Identity Federation would avoid a long-lived credential.
- **Printing plain-text logs from a container** and expecting severity filters or trace correlation to work.
- **Granting Logs Writer to fix wrong severity.** Permissions decide whether entries arrive; the payload format decides how they look.
- **Using averages for latency.** Use percentiles, because averages hide the tail.

## Exam tips

- **Tool matching.** Slow request across microservices means Trace; high CPU or memory in code means Profiler; grouped exceptions mean Error Reporting; business-event alert from logs means a log-based metric.
- **Log-based metric beats export for alerting.** A counter metric on matching entries, then an alerting policy, is the recommended path; BigQuery export is for analysis, not alerting.
- **Central audit retention.** Organization-level aggregated sink to a dedicated, access-controlled destination with the retention you need; `_Required` is fixed at 400 days, `_Default` is 30 days by default.
- **Admin Activity is always on.** Data Access logs are off by default except BigQuery, so enabling them is a deliberate choice with cost.
- **Metrics scope for multi-project views.** One monitoring project can view many projects; use it instead of per-project dashboards.
- **Dashboards are JSON.** Export, strip `name` and `etag`, and apply per project with gcloud or Terraform; viewers of a metrics scope need Monitoring Viewer on the scoping project only.
- **Golden signals.** Latency, traffic, errors, saturation: the first things to put on a user-facing dashboard.
- **Retention numbers.** Trace and Profiler data are kept 30 days; user-defined log buckets can be 1 to 3650 days; locking a bucket is irreversible.
- **Prefer OpenTelemetry** for new tracing instrumentation.
- **Log Analytics is SQL over a log bucket.** Upgrade the bucket and optionally create a linked BigQuery dataset (no ingestion or storage cost) instead of exporting a duplicate copy.
- **Ops Agent is for Compute Engine VMs only.** Fluent Bit for logs, OpenTelemetry Collector for metrics and traces; not needed on GKE, Cloud Run or App Engine, and not supported on on-prem or EC2 hosts.
- **Hybrid telemetry: one plane.** On-prem or other cloud means an OpenTelemetry Collector (Bindplane to manage it), attached clusters with their Fluent Bit DaemonSet, or Managed Service for Prometheus for Prometheus metrics, all feeding Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging.
- **No exported keys off-cloud means Workload Identity Federation.**
- **Structured logs.** One line of JSON on stdout becomes `jsonPayload`; `severity`, `httpRequest` and `logging.googleapis.com/trace` are promoted to LogEntry fields. Plain text becomes `textPayload`, which breaks severity filters and trace correlation.
- **Entries present but wrong means format; entries missing means permissions or limits.** Fix severity in the log format, not with IAM.

diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  S["Symptom in production"] --> H{"What do you need to know?"}
  H -- "Is it healthy or within SLO?" --> M["Cloud Monitoring (metrics, alerts, uptime checks)"]
  H -- "What happened and when?" --> L["Cloud Logging (logs, log-based metrics)"]
  H -- "Which service in the request path is slow?" --> T["Cloud Trace"]
  H -- "Which function burns CPU or memory?" --> P["Cloud Profiler"]
  H -- "Which exceptions are occurring?" --> E["Error Reporting"]
